transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-11-05
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~54 mins
Attendees: Avery (Redwood AE), Morgan (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Priya (Tessera CTO), Miguel (Lead ML), Lina (PM)
---
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone, thanks for joining — we're excited to walk through the action schema and tool orchestration pattern in Redwood, um, 50-ish minute demo and then Q&A. Priya, thanks for the time.
[00:22] Priya: thanks, yeah excited. Quick context: Tessera is building a claims triage flow, we need reliable structured outputs to drive internal ticketing and downstream automations, and security is a big check for us.
[00:40] Morgan: absolutely, that's exactly the pattern we see — structured outputs feeding tool calls is where we can reduce manual error. We'll show JSON mode with schemas, then the Console guardrail UI, then a live tool-call to a sample ticket API.
[01:05] Miguel: quick Q up front — we run on-prem for PHI-sensitive flows. How does the sandbox map to our infra? Dedicated? VPC?
[01:20] Avery: good question — for pilot we usually provision a Dedicated sandbox in your cloud account or our Dedicated pool with VPC peering; private deployment is possible later if you need on-prem air-gap. We'll cover auth/KMS concerns briefly.
[01:36] Jordan: also note Optimize can recommend batching and quantization per-route; for ticketing latency is important so we'll show lower-latency configs.
[01:50] Priya: sounds good. let's do it.
---
Live demo: JSON mode + schema enforcement
[02:10] Morgan: switching to the Console share — on the left is the API playground, middle is our schema editor. I'm going to paste an 'action schema' we use for triage: name, priority (enum), assignee {email}, description, and a 'run_tool' array that maps to function signatures.
[02:42] Morgan: note — in Console you can toggle strict validation (rejects outputs that don't match) or tolerant (emit warning + best-effort map). We'll run strict first.
[03:05] Miguel: can the model call multiple tools in a single response?
[03:12] Morgan: yes — the run_tool array supports multiple entries and we have orchestration hooks so if tool A fails the routing policy can call fallback tool B or raise an error.
[03:28] Avery: also we have prefix caching to speed up repeated prompts, but for small ticket create calls it's not huge.
[03:40] Morgan: starting a test generation — sending prompt: 'Create high-priority ticket for patient claim, summarize key fields and call create_ticket tool with payload'.
[03:58] [03:59] Morgan: the model returns JSON, Console shows it matched the schema, green check. Here's the payload, we'll click 'execute' to invoke the tool binding (we hooked to a stubbed ticket API).
[04:22] Priya: that was slick. Any validation errors surface in-line?
[04:30] Morgan: yes, if the output missing required fields Console highlights them and you can preview an auto-fix suggestion (we call them 'hinted transforms') — this is in tolerant mode.
[04:50] Miguel: what about hallucinated field values, like wrong patient ID?
[04:55] Morgan: two mitigations — one: guardrails and external validators (we can add a post-validate webhook to check IDs), two: function-calling pattern where the model returns a canonical key set and the server-side code verifies and maps before persisting.
---
Function / tool-calling deep-dive
[05:20] Morgan: showing the function signature we registered in the Console: create_ticket(title:string, priority:enum, assignee_email:string, metadata:object). In our demo the model picked priority 'P1' and assigned to 'triage@tessera.com'. We'll show the HTTP request payload.
[05:48] Jordan: we also support signed webhooks and mTLS for tool endpoints so you can run tools behind your network.
[06:05] Priya: what's the retry/backoff model if the ticket API returns 5xx?
[06:10] Morgan: Redwood has policy hooks: on 5xx you can configure retry with exponential backoff, or route to fallback queue; Console has a policy editor.
[06:22] Miguel: in the logs how do we see which model produced which JSON? need traceability for audits.
[06:30] Morgan: per-request tracing with token-level cost/latency and model version tags; we store the raw prompt and output (unless you opt-out for retention). We also emit audit events for every tool call.
---
Guardrails and validation UI
[07:05] Morgan: switching to the guardrail UI — you can set allow-lists, schema strictness, and regex validators per-field. You can also attach unit test prompt sets to run on model versions for regression alerts.
[07:30] Lina: can we enforce redaction for PHI fields?
[07:36] Jordan: yes — redaction policies and KMS-integrated key wrapping; you can configure which fields are persisted. We also support masking in the Console preview.
[07:50] Priya: SOC 2 / ISO?
[07:55] Avery: we have SOC 2 Type II, and enterprise packages include custom audit logging, SSO/SAML, SCIM, and KMS integration. We'll send the security pack after.
---
Optimize recommendations for cost/latency
[08:20] Morgan: moving to Optimize — here's the profile for this workload: many small requests, tight latency SLO. Optimize recommends smaller sequence lengths, CPU-side batching disabled for lowest latency, quantization suggested only for non-critical paths, and prefix-KV caching for repeated patient context. Cost delta estimates are shown.
[08:55] Miguel: so quantization would save cost but possibly increase hallucination?
[09:00] Morgan: sometimes you see slight quality regressions; Optimize flags those and suggests A/B run with a small sample.
---
Live orchestration: failure and fallback example
[09:30] Morgan: we'll demonstrate an intentional failure: the create_ticket tool will return 500 for the first call; Console shows the retry policy firing, then fallback to 'queue_ticket' tool which buffers to a durable queue.
[09:58] [10:00] Priya: awesome—this fallback is important for uptime guarantees.
[10:12] Avery: note in Hosted mode we have multi-region fallback; in Dedicated you can configure route policies to other clusters.
---
Questions / objections
[10:30] Miguel: do we need to change model prompts heavily for JSON mode?
[10:36] Morgan: you will still need to prompt, but JSON mode + schema reduces prompt engineering surface — you supply the schema and instruction like 'output only JSON that conforms to schema'. That plus function signatures gives high determinism.
[10:55] Priya: latency numbers?
[11:00] Morgan: for small outputs with Dedicated GPUs we see ~50-120ms per-token depending on model; Console shows per-route p50/p95. We can run benchmarks against your actual payloads.
[11:20] Lina: any pitfalls when generating arrays of actions?
[11:25] Morgan: arrays are fine but watch token-length explosion; Optimize recommends chunking or streaming the response and validating chunks.
---
Transcription noise / misc notes
[11:50] Miguel: is KV cache the same as K V cash? [laughter]
[12:00] Morgan: yeah transcription will sometimes output K V cash, the runtime uses KV cache.
---
Wrap and recap
[12:10] Avery: quick recap: we demoed the action schema flow in JSON mode, validated outputs with strict/tolerant modes, executed a tool call to create tickets with retries/fallbacks, showed guardrails and Optimize recommendations. Next steps: we'll send the security doc and example schemas, Morgan will provision the sandbox, Priya will send the ticket API spec.
[12:40] Priya: sounds good — we'll aim to have the API spec by 11/9 and ready for the pilot kickoff on 11/12.
[12:50] Avery: great, thanks all. I'll send a follow-up with links to the Console workspace and sample prompts.
[13:00] (call ends)

References / shared artifacts mentioned:
- Demo workspace (Console): https://console.redwood.ai/sandbox/tessera-2025-11 (provisioned post-call)
- Deck: "Action Schemas + Tool Orchestration" (link shared in chat)
- Security pack: sent via email (Avery)

End transcript
